title: Bitcoin Just Crashed Below $70,000 for the First Time Since April. The Sell-Off Has Multiple Triggers.
excerpt: Eleven straight days of ETF outflows, Strategy's first Bitcoin sale in four years, AI stocks vacuuming up liquidity, and Iran tensions have combined to push BTC to its lowest level in two months.
body:
Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Tuesday for the first time since early April, extending a brutal stretch that has wiped out more than 14 per cent of its value in less than three weeks. The largest cryptocurrency was trading near $67,500 in afternoon trading, down nearly 5 per cent on the day, after briefly touching $66,400 — its lowest level since late March.

The sell-off was not caused by a single event. It is the convergence of at least four distinct pressures, each of which would be manageable in isolation but together have created the most hostile environment for crypto since the early months of 2025.

## The ETF Exodus

The most significant driver is the sustained institutional exodus from spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds. US-listed spot BTC ETFs have now recorded 11 consecutive sessions of net outflows, draining more than $4 billion since mid-May. Monday alone saw $484 million leave, according to SoSoValue data.

This matters because the ETFs were the single most important source of new demand for Bitcoin over the past 18 months. When BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) launched in January 2024, it attracted tens of billions in inflows and was widely credited with pushing Bitcoin to record highs. Now the flow has reversed. IBIT shares are down more than 6 per cent on the day.

May is tracking as the third-worst month for Bitcoin ETF flows since launch, with approximately $2.4 billion in net outflows for the month.

## Strategy Sells Bitcoin for the First Time in Four Years

In a move that rattled sentiment far beyond its monetary significance, Strategy — the Michael Saylor-led company that is the world's largest corporate holder of Bitcoin — disclosed that it sold 32 BTC between May 26 and May 31. The average sale price was $77,135 per coin, raising $2.5 million to fund distributions on its preferred stock.

The sale is tiny relative to Strategy's total holdings of 843,706 BTC, purchased at an average cost of $75,699. But the symbolism is powerful. Saylor has spent years positioning himself as Bitcoin's most prominent corporate evangelist, repeatedly saying he would never sell. The fact that his company did sell — for the first time since late 2022 — has undermined the narrative of unconditional institutional conviction.

"Saylor/Strategy selling a few raspberries isn't causing Bitcoin to crash," wrote Pierre Rochard, a Bitcoin researcher and board member at Strive. "The reality is that there is a massive parabolic spike in AI-related equities that is vacuuming up all excess liquidity."

## AI Stocks Are the New Magnet

Rochard's observation touches on what may be the most underappreciated factor in Bitcoin's decline. While crypto has bled, the S&P 500 has posted an eight-session winning streak and closed at fresh record highs on Monday at 7,600. The Nasdaq is at 27,087. Nvidia, fresh off a new chip launch, has pushed the AI trade to euphoric levels.

The divergence is stark. Money that might once have flowed into speculative crypto positions is instead chasing AI infrastructure plays — Nvidia, Marvell Technology (which Jensen Huang just called the "next trillion-dollar company"), Hewlett Packard Enterprise (up sharply on earnings), and Alphabet (which just announced an $80 billion equity raise to fund data centres).

For institutional allocators, the choice between a volatile, yield-free digital asset in a downtrend and an AI sector delivering record earnings growth in an uptrend is not a difficult one. Bitcoin is losing the competition for marginal capital.

## Geopolitics Add Fuel

The backdrop of the Iran conflict continues to weigh on risk appetite selectively. Iran suspended indirect negotiations with the United States on Monday over Israel's military actions in Lebanon, pushing oil prices above $91 a barrel. While gold benefited — climbing 1 per cent to $4,555 an ounce — Bitcoin, which its advocates have long positioned as "digital gold," moved in the opposite direction.

The 10-year Treasury yield dipped to 4.43 per cent, a three-week low. In theory, lower yields should support risk assets. In practice, the flight-to-safety trade is bypassing crypto entirely.

## Derivatives Signal More Pain

Open interest across Bitcoin futures markets has climbed to approximately 773,000 BTC — one of the highest readings on record, according to Coinglass data. Perpetual futures funding rates remain elevated at roughly 10 per cent annualised, meaning long traders are paying to maintain bullish positions even as the spot price falls.

This configuration is a classic setup for cascading liquidations. When leveraged longs are forced to close positions, the selling pressure accelerates the decline, triggering more liquidations in a self-reinforcing loop. More than $766 million in leveraged positions were liquidated in the past 24 hours alone.

## What NRI Investors Should Consider

For Indian diaspora investors — many of whom hold Bitcoin through US-based exchanges, ETFs, or Indian platforms like WazirX and CoinDCX — the current environment demands caution rather than panic.

**If you are holding spot Bitcoin**, the fundamental thesis of scarcity and long-term adoption has not changed. But the near-term technical picture is bearish. Analysts at FXStreet have flagged $65,000 as the next major support level, and a break below that could accelerate losses further.

**If you are holding Bitcoin ETFs**, the outflow data suggests institutional sentiment has turned decisively negative for now. These flows tend to be self-reinforcing — outflows beget more outflows as portfolio managers reduce positions in underperforming assets.

**If you are considering buying the dip**, the derivatives data argues for patience. Elevated open interest and positive funding rates in a falling market mean the flush has not yet happened. Historically, Bitcoin bottoms coincide with capitulation — sharp drops in open interest and negative funding — neither of which has occurred.

**If you hold crypto in India**, remember that Indian tax rules impose a 30 per cent flat tax on crypto gains and a 1 per cent TDS on every transaction above 10,000 rupees. In a declining market, these frictions make it especially costly to trade actively. Buy-and-hold investors face lower tax drag than active traders.

The coming week brings Friday's US payrolls report, which could determine the next directional move. A strong jobs number would keep rate-cut expectations muted and maintain pressure on risk assets. A weaker print could provide the relief rally that leveraged longs are betting on — but that is a bet, not a plan.
